I have an incipient sketch of an equivalence relation:

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Basic

namespace Compartment

def Function.EqvOn {α : Type*} (f : α → α → Prop) (s : Set α) :=
  -- f is reflexive over s
  (∀ x ∈ s, f x x) ∧
  -- f is symmetric in s
  (∀ (x y), x ∈ s → y ∈ s → f x y → f y x) ∧
  -- f is transitive in s
  (∀ (x y z), x ∈ s → y ∈ s → z ∈ s → f x y → f y z → f x z)

def Function.eqv_class {α β : Type*} (f : α → β) (x : α) :=
  {a : α | f a = f x}

def Function.eqv_class_in {α β : Type*} (f : α → β) (s : Set α) (x : α) :=
  {a ∈ s | f a = f x}

def Function.relates {α β : Type*} (f : α → β) (x y : α) :=
  f x = f y

-- Any function induces an equivalence relation:
theorem eqvOn_of_relates {α β : Type*} (s : Set α) (f : α → β)
    : Function.EqvOn (f.relates) s := by
  done

end Compartment

The immediate problem is that the notation f.relates doesn't work. As far as I see, this is because, in order to apply generalized field notation on a function, lean wants me to define the pseudo-field in the Function top-level namespace, whereas this function is defined in the Compartment.Function namespace.

But I have trouble believing this is really the problem, because it seems to completely defeat the purpose of having namespaces. How do I get something that I can use with dot notation without polluting the top-level namespace? I want relates to be projectable onto functions when the Compartment namespace is open, and not otherwise.

(I also have a broader problem: the reason I'm doing this at all is that I wanted to work with equivalence relations, found nothing relevant in Mathematics in Lean, and was able to determine by searching that the relevant part of Mathlib was probably Setoid and Setoid.Partition. But the documentation for Setoid.Partition largely consists of a complaint that it should be "more usable". ( docs#Setoid.eq_of_mem_eqv_class ) So I thought defining my own tools might help me think about what kind of things I want to be able to say. If there's a good guide to the existing way of working with equivalence relations in Mathlib, I wouldn't mind a pointer.)
try doing open Compartment as well (for some reason just being in a namespace Compartment isn't enough)
for equivalence relations, see docs#Equivalence and docs#Setoid

Why do you consider adding definitions to an existing "global" namespace polluting that namespace?

FWIW, Mathlib adds definitions to many namespaces that are from core. For instance, docs#List.toFinmap

fiforeach said:

Why do you consider adding definitions to an existing "global" namespace polluting that namespace?

FWIW, Mathlib adds definitions to many namespaces that are from core. For instance, docs#List.toFinmap

What do you think is the purpose of namespaces as a concept?

They are there to make it possible to use different libraries that provide different things with the same name. If I write a .lean file implementing something called List.toFinmap, and Snir writes a different file implementing something else called List.toFinmap, and you need both things, what's Lean's solution to that?

As far as I can see, there is no solution, and Lean namespaces don't do the only thing namespaces are supposed to do. Is that really the case?

Michael said:

What do you think is the purpose of namespaces as a concept?

The reference says [0]

Namespaces serve to group related definitions, theorems, types, and other declarations.

The flexibility of allowing modules to define names in arbitrary namespaces comes at the cost of being unable to import modules that define the same names. I don't think there is any way to rename/alias names obtained from importing modules.

[0] https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Namespaces-and-Sections/#namespaces

fiforeach said:

The flexibility of allowing modules to define names in arbitrary namespaces comes at the cost of being unable to import modules that define the same names.

That's true everywhere. But in a normal system, it doesn't cause problems because namespaces make it possible for you, the author, to avoid defining the same names that unknown third parties do.

By contrast, requiring definitions that take advantage of generalized field notation to use a global namespace specifically prevents you, the author, from doing that. Here, we are specifically informed that the goal of the language is to get us into conflicts with third parties. Why?
I don't understand what the issue is, lots of languages let you do this. Why are you questioning Lean specifically?

The only languages I know that have some rules against where you define what are C# (for class extension methods specifically, for namespaces you can do whatever) and Rust (orphan rule). Arbitrary namespaces are a common language feature.
I'm complaining that, as far as I can see, arbitrary namespaces are a feature that Lean pretends to have but doesn't actually support. I'm not complaining that it does have arbitrary namespaces.

How do I get something that I can use with dot notation without polluting the top-level namespace? I want relates to be projectable onto functions when the Compartment namespace is open, and not otherwise.

Then it seems we disagree on the meaning of the term "arbitrary namespace".
Regardless of your definition of the term, call it what you will but Lean's namespace keyword works similarly to most languages AFAIK.
How do I put a function that is projectable onto Lists into a namespace that isn't (root).List?
And if I can't do that, if the language requires me to use the specific, unique namespace (root).List, in what sense am I benefiting from the ability to use "arbitrary namespaces"?

I seem to recall there being such a feature, but I'm not sure where I saw it.
Regardless, if that's what you want then it sounds like a feature request, and one that isn't available in most languages AFAIK. IMO criticizing the language is not a productive way to request features.

Michael said:

Lean namespaces don't do the only thing namespaces are supposed to do

What makes you say that your feature request is what namespaces are supposed to do? Is it backed by an existing feature in another language?

Snir Broshi said:

I seem to recall there being such a feature, but I'm not sure where I saw it.

namespace MyNamespace

def List.foo (n : List Nat) : Nat := n.length

end MyNamespace

/-- Invalid field `foo`: The environment does not contain `List.foo` -/
#guard_msgs (substring := true) in
#eval [1, 2, 3].foo

/-- info: 3 -/
#guard_msgs in
open MyNamespace in
#eval [1, 2, 3].foo
I'm not sure why it doesn't work on Function

Interesting! Function is treated differently, since it is not a bona fide type, unlike Nat. (That is, e.g., fun x : Nat => x is not of type Function but rather Nat -> Nat.) So perhaps it could be considered a bug after all...

It seems that lean#6189 which added the feature initially contained special handling for functions to solve lean#1629 but they were reverted (probably in favor of lean#6267). So Function ignoring open might be intended but it might not be.
I think the fix is to change the getEnv.contains in Function handling to resolveGlobalName like normal identifiers use through findMethod?.
cc @Kyle Miller?

The lean#1629 issue has always made Function dot notation problematic. Sometimes I wonder if anything would break if we made dot notation only consider explicit and instance arguments, skipping implicit arguments completely. That would fix Function, and would justify supporting dot notation on it for real.

My understanding why all arguments are considered uniformly is because the main argument for class projections is instance implicit.

Michael said:

I want relates to be projectable onto functions when the Compartment namespace is open, and not otherwise.

It looks like @Snir Broshi already showed open as a solution to this, and that Function is treated differently. Here's a demonstration that in principle the feature works, if it weren't for dot notation on raw functions behaving strangely.

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Rel

def Fn (α β : Type*) := α → β

namespace Compartment

def Function.EqvOn {α : Type*} (f : α → α → Prop) (s : Set α) :=
  -- f is reflexive over s
  (∀ x ∈ s, f x x) ∧
  -- f is symmetric in s
  (∀ (x y), x ∈ s → y ∈ s → f x y → f y x) ∧
  -- f is transitive in s
  (∀ (x y z), x ∈ s → y ∈ s → z ∈ s → f x y → f y z → f x z)

def Fn.eqv_class {α β : Type*} (f : Fn α β) (x : α) :=
  {a : α | f a = f x}

def Fn.eqv_class_in {α β : Type*} (f : Fn α β) (s : Set α) (x : α) :=
  {a ∈ s | f a = f x}

def Fn.relates {α β : Type*} (f : Fn α β) (x y : α) :=
  f x = f y

open Compartment

-- Any function induces an equivalence relation:
theorem eqvOn_of_relates {α β : Type*} (s : Set α) (f : Fn α β)
    : Function.EqvOn f.relates s := by
  simp +contextual [Function.EqvOn, Fn.relates]

end Compartment
But is it intentional that Function is doesn't respect open or is it a bug we can fix? (regardless of lean#1629)
I've gone ahead and made name resolution uniform, and also experimentally added a special case to Function so that dot notation only looks for explicit arguments: lean4#13244

Related to namespaces and generalized field notation iI have come across the following confusing behavior in recursive definitions:

namespace A
-- `open A` does not change the behavior

/--
error: Invalid field `f`: The environment does not contain `Nat.f`, so it is not possible to project the field `f` from an expression
  n
of type `Nat`
-/
#guard_msgs in
def Nat.f : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => n.f + 1

#guard_msgs in
def Nat.g : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | n + 1 => (Nat.g n) + 1

end A

It is particularly confusing because from the point of view of the caller the name Nat.f should exist.
